A drawing is a record of what we notice. One drawing can show where a patch of sunlight falls. It cannot show whether the patch changes position. In this booklet, we will watch the sunlight on our classroom floor and make drawings we can compare.

We will observe over three school days. Work with the same partner each day. Look at the beginning of the morning lesson and immediately after lunch. That gives you six observation spaces. Your drawings will record the position of the light you can see. They will not answer every question about why it is there.

Mark the outline of the light on the printed floor plan. Write the time beside it. If part of the edge is fuzzy, mark that part with a dotted line. You have a pencil and a ruler. A ruler can help you draw a straight line. It cannot make a fuzzy edge sharp. If two groups draw the edge differently, compare what each group noticed before deciding whether either drawing needs to change.

Sometimes there may be no patch to see. Write “no patch visible” in the space for that observation and leave its floor plan unmarked. Yesterday’s patch belongs in yesterday’s drawing. Recording that no patch is visible counts as an observation. It does not give you a measurement of the patch’s position. The curtains will stay in their usual position. We will not control the clouds or record how thick they are.

At the end, compare all six observation spaces with your partner. Write one sentence about a pattern your observations support and one question that remains. If too few patches were visible to establish a pattern, say so. Explain which observations are missing.

There is no particular pattern you must discover. Your booklet needs to show what you could see and what you could not. A careful record of a patch nobody could see can be more useful than a confident drawing of where someone thinks it was.

This release adds **Pause on Focus**, a new option in the desktop application’s **Reading settings**. Turn it on to pause the application’s spoken image description when you move keyboard focus to another control. By default, descriptions continue speaking when focus moves, just as they did before.

When Pause on Focus is enabled, returning focus to the image does not automatically resume the description. Use the existing **Read Description** command to hear it again from the beginning. “Pause” means that speech stops while the saved description is kept; it does not mean you can resume from the word where it stopped. The setting does not change the descriptions themselves.

Pause on Focus works with both automatic descriptions and descriptions you request manually. It does not turn automatic descriptions on. If you previously turned automatic image descriptions off, they will remain off after the update, and you can still use Pause on Focus for manually requested descriptions.

The option controls only image descriptions spoken by the application. A separate screen reader controls its own speech, even when describing the same image, so moving focus may not stop all speech if both are active. Pause on Focus also has no effect on audio inside a video, which remains controlled by the video player. The option is available only on desktop; the mobile version keeps its existing behavior.

If a description continues after keyboard focus has visibly moved, please report it and include the action that moved focus. If you can tell whether the speech came from the application or a separate screen reader, include that too—but you do not need to identify the source before reporting an issue. Knowing what action moved focus is more useful than receiving the contents of the image.

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover might reduce the time water remained above the pavement after rain. Six drains on two streets were observed during four storms before and four storms after a cover change. The three drains on the lower street received new covers; the three on the upper street retained their existing covers. Allocation was not random: crews selected the lower street because it had received more complaints.

Fixed cameras recorded the minutes water remained above a painted reference line at each drain during each storm. All 48 drain-storm observations were available. A recorded duration of zero indicates no visible water above the line, not an absence of runoff. Across the twelve observations for each street in each period, mean duration fell from 18 to 10 minutes on the lower street and from 9 to 7 minutes on the upper street. The lower street therefore showed an eight-minute reduction, compared with a two-minute reduction on the upper street. This larger reduction can inform further study, but the comparison does not by itself establish an effect of the new covers.

Several factors limit interpretation. The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier storms. Neither street had a local gauge, and within-storm rainfall intensity was not measured. Crews also cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. Because the initial quantity of leaves was not recorded, cleaning cannot be assumed to explain the larger improvement on the lower street. Equally, cleaning cannot be dismissed as irrelevant simply because both streets received it. These uncertainties, together with the nonrandom allocation of covers, leave the contribution of the cover change unresolved.

The camera records establish shorter durations above the reference line at both sets of drains during the later period. They do not establish increased drainage capacity, which was not directly measured, or fewer flooded properties, which was not measured at all. The pilot included no property-damage observations. Peak water depth could also change in a way that matters even if duration remained unchanged, but peak depth was not extracted from the images.

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and debris quantities before cleaning. These measures would address some of the present ambiguities, although rotation alone would not make storms identical. The existing recordings remain useful for describing conditions during these eight storms and assessing the practicality of the camera-based duration measure. Staff reported that every recording could be scored; whether different scorers assign the same duration remains untested.

Six drains on two streets were observed during four storms before a cover change and four afterward. Because initial leaf quantities were not recorded, the cleaning could have contributed to the change in durations; the records cannot establish whether it explains the larger reduction on the lower street. Cleaning both streets does not establish that its effects were equal.

Recorded durations above the line were shorter at both sets of drains in the later period. In this hypothetical evaluation, pupils using a worksheet with diagrams beside each question produced a somewhat larger share of fully credited answers than pupils using the same diagrams on a separate reference page. Both worksheet versions asked pupils to explain why the same amount of water looks different in a tall vessel and a wide vessel. Version A placed a diagram beside each question; Version B grouped the same diagrams on a reference page. The wording, diagrams, and question order were otherwise identical. Two classes used A and two used B. Teachers chose their classes’ versions before seeing pupil responses.

The analysis included only returned worksheets: 52 for A and 49 for B. Six additional pupils assigned A and five assigned B were absent. Teachers used the same written instructions but could answer pupils’ questions during the lesson. Those exchanges were not recorded. Neither pupil assignment nor teacher assistance can therefore be treated as controlled by this comparison. No earlier baseline task was scored, so the groups’ starting knowledge is unknown.

A scorer who could not see the worksheet layout assessed transcribed answers to the final explanation question. Answers received one point for stating that the amount of water was unchanged and one for explaining that vessel shape changed the water level.

| One point | 15 | 16 |

These scores describe responses to a single question, rather than pupils’ general understanding of volume. A second scorer assessed ten transcribed answers. Staff time for those checks has not yet been allocated, so the proposal is not ready for unconditional approval.

The signs would provide a public warning; they would not keep water out of the underpass or resolve the drainage problem. Two signs are estimated to cost 18,000 units of local currency, compared with 140,000 for drainage pipe replacement. Neither estimate includes annual maintenance. Signs therefore have a lower initial cost, but they are not a measured substitute for pipe replacement. Without agreed estimates of how much either option would reduce injuries or vehicle damage, the signs should be assessed as a response to delayed warnings, not as a cheaper way to achieve the same outcome.

The signs would activate when a water-level sensor crosses a set threshold. Because the sensor can fail and the signs require power, an unlit sign cannot safely indicate that the road is clear. Installation must include the proposed permanent notice warning drivers that water may be present even when the electronic sign is off. That notice, regular checks and a manual closure procedure address important limitations, but drivers may still overlook or disregard warnings. This limitation does not, by itself, justify rejecting warning equipment.

Pipe replacement remains a separate option requiring design work. Purchasing signs would neither approve nor reject it, and completing the warning project would leave the drainage project unresolved. To address the concern that visible new signs could reduce pressure to improve drainage, require the next infrastructure report to state the pipe project’s status explicitly. This would keep the unresolved work visible; it would not guarantee construction.

I propose revising the report template to make exclusions visible without changing which runs contribute to the reported mean. The summary would show the mean alongside the number of runs attempted and the number retained. A separate table, labeled “Record of exclusions,” would account for the difference by listing each excluded run’s identifier, completion status, reason for exclusion, and whether a usable reading exists. The current summary lists only the runs used to calculate the mean. This makes the mean easy to read, but it prevents readers from distinguishing a batch with no exclusions from one whose exclusions have simply disappeared from view. The proposed table would make those decisions inspectable. It would not require excluded readings to enter the mean or alter the existing exclusion rule.

**Claim.** On a finite probability space, let \(X\) be real-valued and let \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) partition the space. Write \(p_j=P(G_j)\), and define
\[
\mu_j=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{1}{p_j}\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})X(\omega),&p_j>0,\\[6pt]
0,&p_j=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Let \(M=\mu_j\) on \(G_j\). Then, for every real constant \(c\),
\[
E[(X-c)^2]=E[(X-M)^2]+E[(M-c)^2].
\]
Consequently, \(E[(X-c)^2]\ge E[(X-M)^2]\), with equality exactly when \(M=c\) with probability one.

**Proof.** On each cell with \(p_j>0\), the residual has conditional mean zero:
\[
E[X-M\mid G_j]
=\frac{1}{p_j}\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)
=0.
\]
Since \(M-c=\mu_j-c\) is constant on that cell,
\[
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})
\bigl(X(\omega)-M(\omega)\bigr)\bigl(M(\omega)-c\bigr)
=(\mu_j-c)p_jE[X-M\mid G_j]=0.
\]
If \(p_j=0\), every point in \(G_j\) has probability zero, so its contribution to this sum is also zero; no conditional mean on that cell is needed. Summing over all cells gives
\[
E[(X-M)(M-c)]=0.
\]
This uses the zero conditional means and constancy on each cell, without any independence assumption.

Now expand pointwise:
\[
(X-c)^2=(X-M)^2+2(X-M)(M-c)+(M-c)^2.
\]
Taking expectations yields the claimed identity. Finally, \(E[(M-c)^2]\ge0\). Because this expectation is a finite sum of nonnegative terms, it vanishes exactly when \(M=c\) at every point of positive probability, equivalently with probability one. \(\square\)

**Claim.** On a finite probability space \(\Omega\), let \(X\) be a real-valued reading and let \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) partition \(\Omega\) into batch cells. Write \(p_j=\mathbb P(G_j)\) and define
\[
\mu_j=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac{1}{p_j}\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})X(\omega),&p_j>0,\\[6pt]
0,&p_j=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Let \(M=\mu_j\) on \(G_j\). Then, for every real constant \(c\),
\[
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]
=\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]+\mathbb E[(M-c)^2].
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]\geq \mathbb E[(X-M)^2],
\]
with equality exactly when \(M=c\) with probability one.

**Proof.** On each cell with \(p_j>0\), the residual \(X-M\) has conditional mean zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[X-M\mid G_j]
&=\frac{1}{p_j}\sum_{\omega\in G_j}
\mathbb P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)\\
&=\mu_j-\mu_j=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Multiplying by \(p_j\) gives
\[
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}
\mathbb P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)=0.
\]
This sum is also zero when \(p_j=0\), because every point in such a cell has probability zero. Thus the displayed equality holds for every cell without conditioning on a zero-probability event.

Since \(M-c\) is constant on each cell, we can now compute the cross term:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]
&=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{\omega\in G_j}
\mathbb P(\{\omega\})
\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)(\mu_j-c)\\
&=\sum_{j=1}^{m}(\mu_j-c)
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}
\mathbb P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Expanding \(X-c=(X-M)+(M-c)\) and taking expectations therefore yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]
&=\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]
+2\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]
+\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]+\mathbb E[(M-c)^2].
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally,
\[
\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]=\sum_{j=1}^{m}p_j(\mu_j-c)^2\geq0.
\]
This sum vanishes exactly when \(\mu_j=c\) for every cell with \(p_j>0\), which is equivalent to \(M=c\) with probability one. \(\square\)

This uses the residual’s conditional mean zero, with no independence assumption.

Now expand pointwise:
\[
(X-c)^2=(X-M)^2+2(X-M)(M-c)+(M-c)^2.
\]
Taking expectations and using the vanishing cross term proves the identity. Finally, \(E[(M-c)^2]\ge0\), and this finite sum of nonnegative terms is zero exactly when \(M=c\) with probability one. This proves the inequality and its equality condition. \(\square\)

**Claim.** On a finite probability space, let \(X\) be a real-valued reading and let \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) partition the space into batch cells. Write \(p_j=\mathbb P(G_j)\) and define
\[
\mu_j=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac{1}{p_j}\sum_{\omega\in G_j}
\mathbb P(\{\omega\})X(\omega),&p_j>0,\\[6pt]
0,&p_j=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Let \(M=\mu_j\) on \(G_j\). Then, for every real constant \(c\),
\[
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]
=
\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]+\mathbb E[(M-c)^2].
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]\geq \mathbb E[(X-M)^2],
\]
with equality exactly when \(M=c\) with probability one.

**Proof.** We first show that the cross term has expectation zero. On each cell with \(p_j>0\), the conditional mean of \(X-M\) is zero because
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})
\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)
&=
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})X(\omega)
-\mu_jp_j\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(p_j=0\), every point in \(G_j\) has probability zero, so the same sum is zero without dividing by \(p_j\).

Since \(M-c\) is constant on each cell, we can now write
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]
&=\sum_{j=1}^{m}(\mu_j-c)
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})
\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
This uses the zero conditional means and constancy on each cell, with no independence assumption.

Expanding the square and taking expectations gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\bigl((X-M)+(M-c)\bigr)^2\right]\\
&=\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]
+2\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]
+\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]+\mathbb E[(M-c)^2].
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally,
\[
\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]
=\sum_{j=1}^{m}p_j(\mu_j-c)^2\geq0.
\]
This sum is zero exactly when \(\mu_j=c\) for every cell with positive probability, which is equivalent to \(M=c\) with probability one. \(\square\)

**Claim.** Let \(P\) be a real \(d\times d\) matrix, where \(d\geq 1\), satisfying
\[
P^2=P \qquad\text{and}\qquad P^T=P.
\]
Let
\[
S=\{Pz:z\in\mathbb R^d\}
\]
be the subspace of permitted layout displacements. This subspace may be zero-dimensional. For every requested displacement \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), the unique permitted displacement \(y\in S\) minimizing \(\|x-y\|^2\) is \(Px\). More precisely, for every \(y\in S\),
\[
\boxed{\|x-y\|^2=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2,}
\]
where \(\|v\|^2=v^Tv\).

**Proof.** First, \(Px\) belongs to \(S\) by the definition of \(S\). The hypothesis \(P^2=P\) says that applying \(P\) a second time does not change its output. In particular, every permitted displacement \(y=Pz\) satisfies
\[
Py=P(Pz)=P^2z=Pz=y.
\]
Here we substitute \(y=Pz\), use associativity of matrix multiplication, apply \(P^2=P\), and then use \(Pz=y\).

Fix any \(y\in S\). Write
\[
r=x-Px,\qquad q=Px-y.
\]
Thus \(r\) is the residual between the requested displacement and \(Px\), while \(q\) is the difference between \(Px\) and another permitted displacement. By linearity, \(P^2=P\), and \(Py=y\),
\[
Pr=Px-P^2x=0,
\qquad
Pq=P^2x-Py=Px-y=q.
\]

The symmetry hypothesis \(P^T=P\) now shows that these two vectors are perpendicular:
\[
r^Tq
=r^TPq
=(Pr)^Tq
=0.
\]
The first equality uses \(Pq=q\). The second uses
\((Pr)^T=r^TP^T=r^TP\), which is exactly where symmetry is needed. The last uses \(Pr=0\).

Since \(x-y=(x-Px)+(Px-y)=r+q\), expansion gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|x-y\|^2
&=(r+q)^T(r+q)\\
&=r^Tr+2r^Tq+q^Tq\\
&=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The middle line combines the equal scalar cross terms \(r^Tq\) and \(q^Tr\); the last line uses \(r^Tq=0\) and the definitions of \(r\) and \(q\).

The first term in this identity is independent of \(y\). The second is nonnegative and equals zero exactly when \(y=Px\). Because \(Px\in S\), it therefore attains the minimum and is the unique minimizer.

This includes \(P=0\): then \(S=\{0\}\), and the identity becomes \(\|x\|^2=\|x\|^2+0\). It also includes \(P=I\): then \(S=\mathbb R^d\) and the residual is zero. The conclusion concerns squared Euclidean distance to this fixed permitted subspace \(S\).

**Claim.** Let \(P\) be a real \(d\times d\) matrix, where \(d\geq 1\), satisfying
\[
P^2=P,\qquad P^T=P.
\]
Let
\[
S=\{Pz:z\in\mathbb R^d\}
\]
be the subspace of permitted layout displacements. We allow \(S=\{0\}\). For every \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), the unique \(y\in S\) minimizing \(\|x-y\|^2\) is \(Px\). More precisely, for every \(y\in S\),
\[
\|x-y\|^2=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2,
\]
where \(\|v\|^2=v^Tv\).

**Proof.** Fix \(x\in\mathbb R^d\). The vector \(Px\) belongs to \(S\) by definition, so it is a permitted displacement. We will show that choosing any other \(y\in S\) adds exactly \(\|Px-y\|^2\) to the squared distance.

The hypothesis \(P^2=P\) means that applying \(P\) again leaves every vector in \(S\) unchanged. Indeed, if \(y=Pz\), then
\[
Py=P(Pz)=P^2z=Pz=y.
\]
In particular, \(P(Px)=Px\). Thus \(P\) leaves the difference \(Px-y\) unchanged:
\[
P(Px-y)=P(Px)-Py=Px-y.
\]
The same hypothesis shows that \(P\) sends the residual \(x-Px\) to zero:
\[
P(x-Px)=Px-P^2x=Px-Px=0.
\]

We now use the symmetry hypothesis \(P^T=P\) to show that the residual and the difference \(Px-y\) are perpendicular:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(x-Px)^T(Px-y)
&=(x-Px)^TP(Px-y)\\
&=\bigl(P(x-Px)\bigr)^T(Px-y)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first equality uses \(P(Px-y)=Px-y\). The second follows from the transpose rule
\[
\bigl(P(x-Px)\bigr)^T=(x-Px)^TP^T=(x-Px)^TP.
\]
The last equality uses \(P(x-Px)=0\).

Since
\[
x-y=(x-Px)+(Px-y),
\]
expanding the squared Euclidean norm gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|x-y\|^2
&=\|x-Px\|^2
  +2(x-Px)^T(Px-y)
  +\|Px-y\|^2\\
&=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The cross term is zero by the calculation above.

The first term is independent of \(y\), and the second is nonnegative. Choosing \(y=Px\) makes the second term zero and therefore attains the minimum. Any minimizer must satisfy
\[
\|Px-y\|^2=0,
\]
which holds only when \(y=Px\). This proves uniqueness.

The proof also covers \(P=0\), when \(S=\{0\}\) is zero-dimensional. If \(P=I\), then \(S=\mathbb R^d\) and the residual is zero. The conclusion concerns squared distance to the fixed permitted subspace \(S\), not arbitrary layout constraints.

\[
\boxed{\|x-y\|^2=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2,}
\]
where \(\|v\|^2=v^Tv\).

\[
Py=P(Pz)=P^2z=Pz=y.
\]
It follows that
\[
P(Px-y)=P^2x-Py=Px-y.
\]
The same hypothesis shows that \(P\) sends the residual \(x-Px\) to zero:
\[
P(x-Px)=Px-P^2x=Px-Px=0.
\]

The symmetry hypothesis \(P^T=P\) now shows that the residual is perpendicular to \(Px-y\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
(x-Px)^T(Px-y)
&=(x-Px)^TP(Px-y)
&&\text{because }P(Px-y)=Px-y\\
&=\bigl(P(x-Px)\bigr)^T(Px-y)
&&\text{because }P^T=P\\
&=0
&&\text{because }P(x-Px)=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the middle equality, the transpose rule gives
\(\bigl(P(x-Px)\bigr)^T=(x-Px)^TP^T=(x-Px)^TP\).

Finally, write \(x-y=(x-Px)+(Px-y)\). Expanding the squared Euclidean norm gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|x-y\|^2
&=\|x-Px\|^2
  +2(x-Px)^T(Px-y)
  +\|Px-y\|^2\\
&=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2,

Focus lock keeps keyboard focus inside the current dialog until the dialog closes. It is useful when controls behind the dialog remain visible but should not receive keyboard input. Focus lock does not freeze the pointer, and it does not prevent the user from closing the dialog with the documented close command.

The implementation uses a sentinel at each end of the dialog's tab sequence. When focus reaches a sentinel, the handler moves it to the appropriate control at the opposite end. This is a focus-management mechanism, not a security boundary. Code running in the page can still move focus deliberately, so the application must handle those changes rather than assume the lock prevents them.

To test focus lock, open the dialog, traverse its controls in both directions, and close it while focus is on the last control. Focus should return to the control that opened the dialog. If that control has been removed, the application uses its documented fallback target. The fallback is part of the application's behavior and is not chosen by focus lock itself.

A separate hardware example describes a switch whose spring contacts latch when pressed. That use of latch refers to the physical mechanism. The example does not demonstrate the software feature and should not be used as a test of it.

Focus lock can help maintain a predictable keyboard sequence. It does not establish that labels, reading order, or announcements are correct; those require their own checks.

You will need the paper bridge, the tray, and the bag of counters from your group's box. Put the tray in the middle of the table and place the bridge across the tray. The bridge should rest on the two wooden blocks, not on the tray's rim. The tray is there to catch counters if they fall, so check that the tray sits under the middle of the bridge.

Before adding any counters, sketch the bridge from the side. Mark where the bridge touches the blocks. Then put one counter in the centre of the bridge and sketch the bridge again. Your second sketch should show the bridge, including any bend you can see, rather than just the new counter. If you cannot see a bend, say so beside the sketch.

Add counters one at a time, placing each on the same marked spot. After each addition, wait until the bridge stops moving before deciding whether to add another. The counters should stay in the tray if the bridge collapses. Do not rebuild the bridge during this first test, even if you have a promising idea about making it stronger.

When the test ends, count the counters that were on the bridge immediately before the bridge collapsed. If you stop because you have used all twelve counters and the bridge is still standing, record “held twelve; collapse not observed.” That is different from saying the bridge can hold exactly twelve.

Now discuss one change you would like to test next time. Keep your first sketches. Those sketches record what this bridge did before the change, which will be useful when your next bridge behaves differently from the one you imagined.

The listening gallery offers two ways to hear the recorded accounts. You can use the fixed headphones beside each case, or borrow a receiver at the welcome desk to listen through the room’s induction loop. Receivers are free, and no booking is needed. We have six receivers, so one may not be available immediately.

Every recording also has a printed transcript in the drawer beneath its case. The transcripts describe sounds that matter to the account, such as a bell or a pause interrupted by machinery, but not every background sound. Large-print copies are available at the welcome desk. You are welcome to take them into the gallery; please return them before leaving.

At half past each hour, a three-minute sound sequence plays through the room’s speakers. A light above the entrance comes on one minute before it begins. If you would rather avoid the sequence, you can leave through either doorway and return afterward. The recordings at the cases pause during the sequence, then resume from where they stopped.

On Wednesday mornings, from opening until noon, the speaker sequence is switched off. The case recordings and induction loop remain available. These mornings are quieter, but we cannot promise silence: people still talk, doors open, and school groups sometimes visit.

You are welcome to ask a gallery host for help with the equipment or for a seat. Hosts can explain the available options, though they cannot reserve a receiver or keep the room quiet for an individual visit. If you prefer to read before coming, you can request the same transcripts from the visitor team.

Of the 600 households invited to our library-use survey, 360 returned the initial questionnaire. Among these respondents, 252 reported using a library in the previous month: 70 percent. This figure described the initial respondents, as the preliminary note stated. It did not establish the percentage among all invited households, although it was sometimes interpreted that way.

The telephone follow-up added information from 90 of the 240 initial nonrespondents. Interviewers stopped when they reached the budgeted total of 90 completed interviews. These households were not a simple random sample of the initial nonrespondents: inclusion depended on whether interviewers could reach them and whether they agreed to participate. Of the 90, 42 reported library use in the previous month, or approximately 46.7 percent.

Combining the two stages gives 294 reports of library use among 450 responding households, or approximately 65.3 percent. The decline from 70 to 65.3 percent shows how the descriptive result changed when the follow-up households joined the respondent pool. The follow-up respondents reported library use less often than the initial respondents. Although both stages used the same question and reference month, households were not randomly assigned to questionnaire or telephone modes. We therefore cannot separate differences between the people reached from any effect of how the question was administered.

The follow-up broadened the observed group, but it did not establish that nonresponse had been corrected. No weights or imputed responses were used, and 150 households still provided no response. We do not know whether those households resemble either responding group. Treating the combined percentage as an estimate for all 600 invitees would require assumptions that this study did not evaluate.

The report should retain the results from both stages and present 65.3 percent as the percentage among all responding households. This preserves the follow-up’s concrete contribution—additional responses that changed the observed result—while making clear that library use among all invited households remains unknown.

We started by counting filled date fields because they seemed a simple way to measure completeness. But a year in the field was not enough. It also needed to be supported by the card. An empty field could mean that the date was unreadable, that there was no date, or that someone had missed it. Before using completeness as a measure, we needed to separate those possibilities.

We chose eighty catalogue cards from one drawer that had not yet been entered into the digital index. Two staff members transcribed each card independently. They could enter a year, mark the date as absent, or mark it as unreadable. The instructions did not allow them to infer a year. We later inspected the cards together and recorded a reference decision for each one. This gave us an internally reconciled record for the trial, rather than an independent external check of the dates.

In that record, fifty cards had a readable year, eighteen had no date, and twelve had an unreadable date. The first transcriber entered the reference year on forty-seven of the fifty readable cards and marked the other three as unreadable. The second entered the reference year on forty-nine and marked one as unreadable. Neither entered a year on any of the thirty cards recorded as having an absent or unreadable date. On those thirty cards, the transcribers agreed with each other about whether the date was absent or unreadable on twenty-six. We have not counted how often each transcriber agreed with the reconciled decision on that distinction.

Counting only cards with a year would make both transcribers’ work look substantially incomplete. Yet for thirty cards, the instructions required an entry other than a year. That count would also leave out the four disagreements about why no year was entered. Those differences matter to the next person using the record. A reader trying to find a document’s date needs to know something different from a conservator considering whether another imaging method might help.

We chose the drawer for convenience, so these counts describe this trial only. They do not estimate error across the collection. They suggest that we should report readable-year transcription separately from decisions about absent or unreadable dates. That would make clearer what we had counted. Whether it would help people retrieve items later remains untested.

The second entered the reference year on forty-nine and marked one as unreadable. Neither entered a year on any of the thirty cards recorded as having an absent or unreadable date. On those thirty cards, the transcribers agreed with each other about the reason on twenty-six. We have not counted how often each transcriber’s choice between absent and unreadable matched the reconciled decision.

Counting only fields containing a year would make both transcribers’ work look substantially incomplete. Yet on thirty cards, the procedure required an entry other than a year. The same count would also hide the four cards on which the transcribers disagreed about why no year could be entered. Those reasons matter for what happens next. A reader trying to find a document’s date needs different information from a conservator considering whether another imaging method might help.

We chose the drawer for convenience, so these counts describe this trial. They do not estimate error across the collection. They suggest that we should report readable-year transcription separately from decisions about absent and unreadable dates. Whether that change helps people retrieve material remains a question for later work. We have not tested it.

We started by counting dates entered in the index, but that count could not tell us whether the work was complete. A blank field might mean that the date was unreadable, that the card had no date, or that someone had missed it. A filled field did not by itself show that the item supported the date. We needed to distinguish these cases before deciding what to count.

We selected eighty catalogue cards from a single drawer that had not yet been entered into the digital index. Two staff members transcribed each card independently. They could enter a year, mark the date as absent, or mark it as unreadable. The instructions did not allow them to infer a year. A later joint inspection established a reference decision for each card. This gave us an internal reconciliation for the trial, not an independent external validation of the dates.

The first transcriber entered the reference year on forty-seven of the fifty readable cards and marked the other three as unreadable. The second entered the reference year on forty-nine and marked one as unreadable. Neither entered a year on any of the thirty cards classified as absent or unreadable in the reconciled record. On those thirty cards, they agreed with each other about whether the date was absent or unreadable on twenty-six. We have not tabulated how often each transcriber agreed with the reconciled decision on that distinction.

Judging the work only by the proportion of cards containing a year would make both transcribers appear to have left much of it incomplete. Yet the procedure required a different entry when a date was absent or unreadable. Counting years alone would also hide the four disagreements about why no year was entered. Those distinctions could guide later work. A reader trying to find a document’s date needs different information from a conservator considering whether another imaging method might help.

We chose the drawer for convenience, so these counts describe the trial rather than estimate error across the collection. They suggest that we should report readable-year transcription separately from decisions about absent or unreadable dates. We have not tested whether reporting them separately improves later retrieval.

We recommend repeating the pond survey this season before describing this year’s lower count as a population decline. These recommendations are consistent: we can act promptly to improve the evidence while remaining cautious about what the existing count means.

Last year’s team visited each of eight ponds twice at dusk. This year’s team visited the same ponds once at midday and recorded fewer animals overall. No adjustment has been made for the differences in visit frequency or time of day, and the records do not contain enough information to reconstruct the missed dusk visits. The lower total is an observation that warrants attention, but the difference between the totals does not establish whether, or by how much, the population has declined.

The pending drainage proposal adds urgency to the monitoring decision. It concerns three of the surveyed ponds, and the advisory meeting is next month. Because drainage has not begun, the proposal does not explain this year’s lower count. It does, however, make information about the ponds’ condition relevant to an upcoming decision. That urgency does not make the two surveys more comparable.

We recommend two dusk visits to each pond, using last year’s recording sheet. Matching those features would reduce an avoidable source of ambiguity and make the new observations more comparable with last year’s. Weather and detectability would still vary, however. The repeat survey would neither isolate the effect of drainage nor provide a population census. Its immediate purpose is to improve the evidence available to the meeting.

If the repeat survey cannot be completed before the meeting, the advisory note should report the lower observed total together with the differences in survey effort and timing, and identify the planned work as pending. The current record supports neither a confident estimate of decline nor a confident assurance of stability. The monitoring request should be judged by its value to the pending decision, without requiring either conclusion in advance.

We recommend keeping completed interviews in the weekly dashboard while ending the practice of ranking interviewers by that number alone. The count tells us whether fieldwork is moving, but it does not tell us enough to compare people whose assigned routes differ.

Some routes contain apartment buildings with a staffed entrance. Others contain scattered homes that require long walks between attempts. Although assignments rotate each month, the dashboard ranks interviewers each week. Rotation may spread difficult routes over a longer period without making any particular week’s assignments comparable. We have not estimated how large that difference is.

The ranking also leaves out work that does not produce a completed interview. A careful refusal record or a return visit at the requested time may be necessary fieldwork even when no completed questionnaire results. Including those activities in the discussion would not mean treating every attempt as equally useful. Supervisors would still need to look at what happened and whether the agreed contact procedure was followed.

We do not propose replacing the ranking with a single weighted score. We have no tested weights, and a score could conceal the same judgment inside a formula. Instead, for the next four weeks, the dashboard should show completed interviews, attempts, and route assignments together, with supervisors adding a brief explanation when discussing unusual totals.

This arrangement will take more attention than reading a league table, and that cost is part of the recommendation. It may also reveal problems that the old ranking missed, but we cannot claim that it will improve response rates before trying it. At the end of four weeks, the steering group should ask whether the added context led to useful changes in supervisory decisions and whether the burden was manageable. The aim is to make the weekly discussion more informative while preserving a clear view of fieldwork progress.

Let \(N\ge 2\), and let \(y_1,\ldots,y_N\) be fixed real responses. Define
\[
\mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N y_i,
\qquad
\sigma^2=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mu)^2.
\]
Choose an unordered pair \(P\) uniformly from the \(\binom N2\) pairs, then choose \(J\) uniformly from the two indices in \(P\). Set
\[
Y=y_J,
\qquad
Z=\frac12\sum_{i\in P}y_i.
\]
All expectations and variances below refer to this sampling procedure; the population responses are fixed. We show that
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]

Each index \(i\) belongs to \(N-1\) pairs. Thus
\[
\Pr(J=i)=\frac{N-1}{\binom N2}\cdot\frac12=\frac1N.
\]
Consequently, \(Y\) is a uniformly sampled population response, so
\[
\mathbb E[Y]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2.
\]

Conditional on \(P=\{i,j\}\), the variable \(Y\) takes the values \(y_i\) and \(y_j\) with equal probabilities, while \(Z=(y_i+y_j)/2\) is fixed. Hence
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z,
\qquad
\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]=0.
\]
Averaging the first identity over the possible pairs gives
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[Y\mid P]\right]
=\mathbb E[Y]=\mu.
\]

To obtain the variance, write
\[
Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu).
\]
The cross term has expectation zero. Indeed, conditioning on \(P\) makes \(Z-\mu\) a fixed multiplier, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)\mid P]\right]\\
&=\mathbb E\!\left[(Z-\mu)\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]\right]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Squaring the decomposition and taking expectations therefore yields
\[
\sigma^2
=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z).
\]
This step uses the zero conditional mean of \(Y-Z\), not independence of \(Y\) and \(Z\).

For a given pair \(P=\{i,j\}\), the two possible values of \(Y-Z\) are \((y_i-y_j)/2\) and its negative. Therefore,
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
\]
Averaging over the uniformly chosen pairs gives
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
=\frac{1}{4\binom N2}\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2.
\]
Expanding the squared differences establishes the finite-population identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
&=N\sum_i y_i^2-\left(\sum_i y_i\right)^2\\
&=N\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2
=N^2\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows that
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]=\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)},
\]
and hence
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(Z)
=\sigma^2-\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)}
=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.}
\]

When \(N=2\), the pair contains the entire population and \(Z=\mu\) is constant. If all responses coincide, both variances vanish for every \(N\). The argument covers these cases without dividing by \(\sigma^2\).

The case contains a facsimile of the workshop ledger. The original is kept in controlled storage because repeated exposure to light would make its faded entries harder to read. A facsimile reproduces a particular object; a reconstruction attempts to supply something missing. This display uses the first approach. Gaps in the original remain gaps in the copy.

The pages are reproduced at their original size. The paper is modern and has not been artificially aged. We chose it for contrast and durability, not to make a visitor believe it had survived a century in the workshop. A small label on every opening identifies the copy, so visitors who enter halfway along the case receive the same information as those who start at the beginning.

The transcription beside the facsimile expands common abbreviations in square brackets. An uncertain reading is followed by a question mark. These conventions separate a proposed reading from a clear one, but they cannot convey every hesitation made during transcription. Readers who want to compare the handwriting can use the facing image.

A two-week trial of the display has ended. During the trial, hosts recorded which labels visitors asked about and whether visitors noticed that the ledger was a copy. The observations will be discussed now that the trial has ended. They will inform a later decision about the labels; the trial itself does not commit the museum to changing them.

At the start of each shift, place the probe in the reference fixture and record its reading. The acceptance band is 48 to 52 units, including both endpoints. This check compares the probe with a stable reference block. It does not measure the temperature of material currently on the line, and a reading inside the band does not by itself authorize a production restart.

During the six-week trial, if the first reference-block reading is outside the acceptance band, let the probe rest in the fixture for ten minutes, then repeat the reading once. The rest period applies only before the repeat; the start-of-shift check and acceptance band are unchanged. Record both readings in the shift log before making any required call. If the repeat is also outside the band, call the shift lead, who will decide whether a further check is needed. If the repeat is within the band, no call is required by this rule. Do not change the probe's offset in response to this check. The trial concerns the escalation process, not permission for operators to recalibrate the instrument.

For the weekly trend chart, use the first reading from each shift, including first readings outside the acceptance band. Keep any repeat readings in the log, but do not substitute them into the chart. This keeps the plotted sequence tied to the same point in the checking process, even when the escalation procedure calls for more than one observation.

The maintenance team will review the log and the chart at the end of the trial. A charted outlier is a reason to examine the record, not a diagnosis of a failed probe. Please include notes about a loose fixture or an interrupted check where relevant. Those notes help explain what happened, but they do not replace the numerical readings.

One drawing shows where we saw a patch of sunlight. It cannot show whether the patch changes position. Over three school days, we will watch where sunlight falls on the classroom floor. You will work with the same partner each day and observe twice: at the beginning of the morning lesson and immediately after lunch. Your drawings will record where you can see the light. They will not answer every question about why it is there.

Mark the outline of the light on the printed floor plan and write the time beside it. Use a dotted line for any part of the edge that looks fuzzy. A pencil and ruler are provided. The ruler can help you draw a straight line, but it cannot tell you exactly where a fuzzy edge ends. If two groups mark an edge differently, compare what you noticed before deciding whether either drawing needs to change.

Sometimes there may be no patch to see. Write “no patch visible” in the space for that observation and leave the floor plan unmarked. Do not draw the patch where it was yesterday. You have recorded what you could see, but you have not measured the patch’s position. The curtains will stay in their usual position. We will not control the clouds or record how thick they are.

At the end, compare all six observation spaces with your partner. Write one sentence about a pattern your observations support and one question that remains. If too few patches were visible to establish a pattern, say so and explain which observations are missing. You do not have to find a particular pattern. A careful record of what you could not see can be more useful than a confident drawing of a patch nobody saw.

This release adds Pause on Focus, a new option in the desktop application’s Reading settings. Turn it on to pause a spoken image description when you move keyboard focus to another control. The default behavior stays the same: descriptions continue speaking when focus moves.

Returning focus to the image does not resume the description automatically. To hear it again from the beginning, use the existing Read Description command. “Pause” means speech stops while the saved description is kept. Playback cannot resume from the word where it stopped, and the setting does not change the descriptions themselves.

Pause on Focus works with both automatic descriptions and descriptions you request manually. It does not turn automatic descriptions on: if you have them turned off, they will stay off after updating. You can still use the new option to pause descriptions you request manually.

The option controls only descriptions spoken by the application. A separate screen reader controls its own speech, even when describing the same image, and audio inside a video remains controlled by the video player. If more than one source of speech is active, some speech may therefore continue after focus moves. Pause on Focus is available only on desktop. The mobile version keeps its existing behavior.

If a description continues after focus has visibly moved, please report it. If you can tell whether the speech came from the application or a separate screen reader, include that detail, but you do not need to identify the source to report the issue. Telling us what action moved focus is more useful than sending the contents of the image.

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover might reduce the time water remained above the pavement after rain. Six drains on two streets were observed during four storms before a cover change and four storms afterward. The three drains on the lower street received new covers, while the three on the upper street retained their existing covers. Crews chose the lower street because it had received more complaints, so allocation was not random.

For each drain during each storm, a fixed camera recorded the number of minutes water remained above a painted reference line. A duration of zero indicates no visible water above that line, not an absence of runoff. All 48 drain-storm observations were available. Across the twelve observations in each period, the mean duration on the lower street fell from 18 minutes before the change to 10 minutes afterward. On the upper street, it fell from 9 minutes to 7 minutes. The lower street therefore had a larger reduction: eight minutes compared with two. This difference may help guide further study, but it does not by itself establish an effect of the covers.

Two other changes complicate the comparison. The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier storms. Neither street had a rain gauge, and no within-storm intensity measurements were available. Crews also cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. Because the amount of debris present before cleaning was not recorded, the contribution of cleaning to the larger reduction on the lower street remains unresolved. Cleaning both streets neither establishes that cleaning explains the difference nor rules out its contribution.

The camera records establish that water remained above the reference line for less time at both sets of drains during the later period. They do not directly measure drainage capacity. Flooded properties were not measured, and the pilot included no property-damage observations. Duration also does not capture every potentially relevant change in water levels: peak depth could change even if duration stayed the same, but peak depth was not extracted from the images.

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and debris before cleaning. These steps could help distinguish cover effects from differences in rainfall and debris, although rotation alone would not make storms identical. The existing recordings remain useful for describing the eight observed storms and assessing whether the camera-based duration measure is practical. Staff reported that every recording could be scored, but agreement between different scorers has not been tested.

## Findings

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover might reduce the time water remained above the pavement after rain. We observed six drains on two streets during four storms before a cover change and four storms afterward. Covers were changed at the three drains on the lower street; the three drains on the upper street kept their covers. Crews had received more complaints about the lower street, so the cover assignment was not random.

For each drain and storm, a fixed camera recorded the number of minutes water was visible above a painted reference line. A duration of zero means no visible water above that line; it does not mean the drain received no runoff. All 48 drain-storm observations were available. Across the twelve observations from each street in each period, mean recorded duration on the lower street fell from 18 minutes before the change to 10 minutes afterward. On the upper street, it fell from 9 to 7 minutes. The reduction was greater on the street where covers changed. That difference may help guide what to study next, but this comparison alone cannot identify an effect of the covers.

The later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier storms. There were no gauges on either street and no measurements of rainfall intensity during individual storms. Crews also cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers changed. Because the initial quantity of leaves was not recorded, the cleaning could have contributed to the results, but the available evidence does not show whether it explains why recorded durations fell more on the lower street. The fact that both streets were cleaned does not establish that cleaning was irrelevant.

Recorded durations above the reference line were shorter at both sets of drains in the later period. The pilot did not directly measure drainage capacity or the number of flooded properties, and it collected no property-damage observations. Peak water depth could change even when duration above the line does not, but peak depth was not extracted from the images.

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and debris before cleaning. These steps would address some of the current uncertainties, though rotating covers would not make storms identical. The existing recordings can describe the eight observed storms and help assess whether camera-based duration measurement is practical. Staff reported that all recordings could be scored. The study did not test whether different scorers would assign the same durations.

This evaluation compared two worksheet layouts for a task asking pupils to explain why the same amount of water looks different in a tall vessel and a wide vessel. Version A placed a diagram beside each question. Version B grouped the same diagrams on a reference page. The wording, diagrams, and question order were otherwise identical. Four classes used the worksheets during one lesson, with two classes using each version. Teachers chose the version for their classes before seeing pupils’ responses.

The analysis included 52 returned worksheets for A and 49 for B. Six additional pupils assigned A and five assigned B were absent. Only returned worksheets were analysed. Teachers used the same written instructions but could answer pupils’ questions during the lesson. Those exchanges were not recorded. The comparison therefore did not control either which pupils used each version or the assistance they received.

A scorer assessed transcribed answers to the final explanation question without seeing the worksheet layout. Answers received one point for stating that the amount of water was unchanged and one for explaining that the vessel’s shape changed the water level.

| Score on the final question | Version A | Version B |
|---|---:|---:|
| Two points | 31 | 27 |
| One point | 15 | 16 |
| Zero points | 6 | 6 |
| Total returned worksheets | 52 | 49 |

These scores describe responses to one question, rather than pupils’ general understanding of volume. A second scorer assessed ten transcribed answers. The scorers agreed on nine, and discussion resolved the tenth before the final totals were compiled. This small check helps describe how the scoring was carried out but does not amount to a complete reliability study. No earlier baseline task was scored, so the groups’ starting knowledge is unknown.

The layout with diagrams beside each question was associated with a somewhat larger share of fully credited answers: 31 of 52 for A, compared with 27 of 49 for B. However, the evaluation cannot establish whether that difference was due to layout, differences between classes, or classroom assistance. It also provides no evidence about which layout pupils preferred, because no preference question was asked. The completed evaluation provides a concrete comparison of the returned answers, with the conclusions limited by what was controlled and recorded.

## Classroom materials evaluation

The evaluation compared two versions of a worksheet asking pupils to explain why the same amount of water looks different in a tall vessel and a wide vessel. Version A placed a diagram beside each question. Version B put the same diagrams together on a reference page. The wording, diagrams, and question order were otherwise identical.

Four classes used the materials in one lesson. Two classes received each version. Teachers chose their classes’ versions before seeing pupil responses. We received 52 worksheets for A and 49 for B. Six pupils assigned A and five assigned B were absent. The analysis included returned worksheets only. Teachers gave the same written instructions, but could answer pupils’ questions during the lesson. Those exchanges were not recorded, so neither pupil assignment nor teacher assistance was controlled by the worksheet comparison.

A scorer who could not see the worksheet layout assessed transcribed answers to the final explanation question. The scoring rule gave one point for saying the amount of water was unchanged and one for explaining that the vessel’s shape changed the water level. Both points were awarded on 31 of 52 A worksheets and 27 of 49 B worksheets. One point was awarded on 15 A worksheets and 16 B worksheets. The remaining six worksheets in each group received zero. These scores describe answers to one question, not pupils’ general understanding of volume.

A second scorer rescored ten transcribed answers. The scorers agreed on nine. They discussed the tenth answer and resolved it before compiling the final totals. This small check documents the scoring procedure, but it is not a complete reliability study. We did not score an earlier baseline task, so the groups’ starting knowledge is unknown.

In these classes, the side-by-side layout was associated with a somewhat larger share of fully credited answers. The evaluation cannot separate the layout’s association from class differences or classroom assistance. It also cannot show which layout pupils preferred, since no preference question was asked. The results provide a comparison of the returned answers from these classes and indicate that a more controlled evaluation would need to record classroom assistance and account for class differences.

We should install the proposed automatic warning signs to address the delay between water entering the underpass and a maintenance crew closing the road. Approval should depend on naming a team responsible for monthly sensor checks, allocating staff time for those checks, and providing a manual closure procedure for when the system is unavailable. Staff time has not yet been allocated, so the purchase is not ready for approval.

The signs would warn drivers about flooding. They would not keep water out of the underpass or resolve the drainage project. Installing two signs is estimated to cost 18,000 units of local currency, compared with 140,000 for replacing the drainage pipe. Neither estimate includes annual maintenance, and we have no agreed estimate of how much either option would reduce injuries or vehicle damage. The signs are a smaller initial purchase, but that does not make them a cheaper way to achieve the same outcome as pipe replacement. They should be assessed for their role in addressing delayed warnings.

The signs would activate when a water-level sensor crosses a set threshold. The sensor can fail, and the signs need power, so an unlit sign cannot safely indicate that the road is clear. The proposal therefore includes a permanent notice warning drivers that water may be present even when the electronic sign is off. That notice cannot prevent drivers from overlooking or disregarding warnings. These limitations make maintenance and manual closure arrangements necessary, but the inability to prevent every unsafe entry is not, by itself, a reason to reject warning equipment.

Pipe replacement remains a separate option requiring design work. Purchasing signs would neither approve nor reject it. There is a reasonable concern that a visible new device could reduce pressure to address the drainage. To address that concern in part, the next infrastructure report should explicitly state the pipe project's status. This would keep the unresolved drainage work visible, though it would not guarantee construction.

I recommend installing the proposed automatic warning signs, provided the same decision names a team responsible for monthly sensor checks and establishes a manual road-closure procedure for when the system is unavailable. I propose adding a separate table of excluded runs to the report template and showing the number of runs attempted and retained beside the reported mean. The table would account for the difference between those counts. At present, the final summary lists only the runs used to calculate the mean. That makes the mean easy to read, but leaves readers unable to tell whether a batch had no exclusions or whether excluded runs were simply omitted from the summary.

The table would document how our existing exclusion rule was applied, without changing which runs enter the mean. For example, a run stopped because the temperature controller failed did not meet the stated measurement conditions. A completed run with an unusual result is different: the result alone does not establish that the conditions failed. Our existing rule excludes controller failures and retains unusual completed results unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies exclusion. Recording both the exclusion and its reason would let readers inspect those decisions.

- Completion status
- Reason for exclusion
- Whether a usable reading exists

**Claim.** On a finite probability space \(\Omega\), let \(X\) be real-valued and let \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) partition \(\Omega\) into batch cells. Write \(p_j=\mathbb P(G_j)\) and define
\[
\mu_j=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac{1}{p_j}\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})X(\omega),&p_j>0,\\[6pt]
0,&p_j=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Let \(M=\mu_j\) on \(G_j\). Then, for every real constant \(c\),
\[
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]
=\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]+\mathbb E[(M-c)^2].
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]\geq \mathbb E[(X-M)^2],
\]
with equality exactly when \(M=c\) with probability one.

**Proof.** On each cell with \(p_j>0\), the residual \(X-M\) has conditional mean zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[X-M\mid G_j]
&=\frac{1}{p_j}\sum_{\omega\in G_j}
\mathbb P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)\\
&=\mu_j-\mu_j\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
We use this fact to compute the cross term. Since \(M-c\) is constant on each cell,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]
&=\sum_{j=1}^m(\mu_j-c)
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})
\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)\\
&=\sum_{j:\,p_j>0}(\mu_j-c)p_j
\mathbb E[X-M\mid G_j]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The second line omits the cells with \(p_j=0\): every point in such a cell has probability zero, so its inner sum is zero. No conditional expectation on those cells is needed.

Now expand pointwise:
\[
\begin{aligned}
X-c&=(X-M)+(M-c),\\
(X-c)^2&=(X-M)^2+2(X-M)(M-c)+(M-c)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking expectations and using the vanishing cross term gives
\[
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]
=\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]+\mathbb E[(M-c)^2].
\]
Finally,
\[
\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]=\sum_{j=1}^m p_j(\mu_j-c)^2\geq0.
\]
This sum is zero exactly when \(\mu_j=c\) for every cell with \(p_j>0\), which is equivalent to \(M=c\) with probability one. \(\square\)

\mathbb P(\{\omega\})X(\omega), & p_j>0,\\[6pt]
0, & p_j=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Let \(M(\omega)=\mu_j\) for \(\omega\in G_j\). Then, for every real constant \(c\),
\[

=

\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]\geq \mathbb E[(X-M)^2],
\]
with equality exactly when \(M=c\) with probability one.

**Proof.** On each cell with \(p_j>0\), \(M\) is the conditional mean of \(X\), so the residual has conditional mean zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[X-M\mid G_j]
&=\frac{1}{p_j}\sum_{\omega\in G_j}
\mathbb P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)\\
&=\frac{p_j\mu_j-p_j\mu_j}{p_j}\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(p_j=0\), every point in \(G_j\) has probability zero. Thus, without defining a conditional expectation on such a cell, we have for every \(j\),
\[
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}
\mathbb P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)=0.
\]

Because \(M-c\) is constant on each cell, we can factor it out of the corresponding sum:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]
&=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{\omega\in G_j}
\mathbb P(\{\omega\})
\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)(\mu_j-c)\\
&=\sum_{j=1}^{m}(\mu_j-c)
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}
\mathbb P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now expand pointwise:
\[
\begin{aligned}
X-c&=(X-M)+(M-c),\\
(X-c)^2&=(X-M)^2+2(X-M)(M-c)+(M-c)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking expectations and using the vanishing cross term gives the identity.

Finally,
\[
\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]=\sum_{j=1}^{m}p_j(\mu_j-c)^2\geq0.
\]
This sum is zero exactly when \(\mu_j=c\) for every cell with \(p_j>0\), which is equivalent to \(M=c\) with probability one. \(\square\)

**Claim.** On a finite probability space, let \(X\) be real-valued and let \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) partition the space into batch cells. Write \(p_j=\mathbb P(G_j)\) and define
\[
\mu_j=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac{1}{p_j}\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})X(\omega),
& p_j>0,\\[6pt]
0,&p_j=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Let \(M=\mu_j\) on \(G_j\). Then, for every real constant \(c\),
\[
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]
=
\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]+\mathbb E[(M-c)^2].
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]\geq \mathbb E[(X-M)^2],
\]
with equality exactly when \(M=c\) with probability one.

**Proof.** On each cell with \(p_j>0\), \(M=\mu_j\) is the conditional mean of \(X\). Thus the weighted sum of the residuals on that cell is zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})
\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)
&=
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})X(\omega)
-\mu_jp_j\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(p_j=0\), every point in \(G_j\) has probability zero, so the same sum is zero.

Since \(M-c\) is constant on each cell, we can factor it out of the corresponding sum:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]
&=
\sum_{j=1}^{m}(\mu_j-c)
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})
\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
This uses the conditional mean on each cell and requires no independence assumption.

Now expand pointwise:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(X-c)^2
&=\bigl((X-M)+(M-c)\bigr)^2\\
&=(X-M)^2+2(X-M)(M-c)+(M-c)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking expectations and using the vanishing cross term gives the identity.

Finally,
\[
\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]
=\sum_{j=1}^{m}p_j(\mu_j-c)^2\geq0.
\]
This sum is zero exactly when \(\mu_j=c\) for every cell of positive probability. Cells of probability zero impose no restriction, so this is equivalent to \(M=c\) with probability one. \(\square\)

**Proof.** Since all expectations are finite sums, we can sum over the cells of the partition. On each cell \(G_j\) with \(p_j>0\), \(M=\mu_j\), so
\[
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})(X(\omega)-M(\omega))
=\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})X(\omega)-p_j\mu_j
=0.
\]
Cells with \(p_j=0\) contribute nothing to any expectation, since every \(\omega\in G_j\) has \(P(\{\omega\})=0\). Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]
&=\sum_{j:p_j>0}(\mu_j-c)
  \sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})(X(\omega)-M(\omega))\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Pointwise, \(X-c=(X-M)+(M-c)\). Squaring and taking expectations gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]
&=\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]
  +2\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]
  +\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]+\mathbb E[(M-c)^2].
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \((M-c)^2\ge 0\), the identity implies
\(\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]\ge \mathbb E[(X-M)^2]\). Equality holds exactly when \((M-c)^2=0\) with probability one, or equivalently when \(M=c\) with probability one.

**Claim.** Let \(P\) be a real \(d\times d\) matrix, where \(d\geq 1\), satisfying
\[
P^2=P
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
P^T=P.
\]
Let
\[
S=\{Pz:z\in\mathbb R^d\}
\]
be the subspace of permitted layout displacements. For every \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), the unique \(y\in S\) minimizing \(\|x-y\|^2\) is \(Px\). More precisely, for every \(y\in S\),
\[
\|x-y\|^2=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2,
\]
where \(\|v\|^2=v^Tv\).

**Proof.** The candidate \(Px\) belongs to \(S\) by its definition. The hypothesis \(P^2=P\) says that applying \(P\) a second time leaves its output unchanged. In particular, if \(y\in S\), then \(y=Pz\) for some \(z\in\mathbb R^d\), so
\[
Py=P(Pz)=P^2z=Pz=y.
\]
Thus \(P\) leaves both \(Px\) and \(y\) unchanged, and hence
\[
P(Px-y)=P^2x-Py=Px-y.
\]
The same hypothesis shows that \(P\) sends the residual \(x-Px\) to zero:
\[
P(x-Px)=Px-P^2x=0.
\]

We now use the symmetry hypothesis \(P^T=P\) to show that the residual is perpendicular to \(Px-y\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
(x-Px)^T(Px-y)
&=(x-Px)^TP(Px-y)\\
&=\bigl(P(x-Px)\bigr)^T(Px-y)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first equality uses \(P(Px-y)=Px-y\). For the second, symmetry gives
\[
\bigl(P(x-Px)\bigr)^T=(x-Px)^TP^T=(x-Px)^TP.
\]
The last equality uses \(P(x-Px)=0\).

Since
\[
x-y=(x-Px)+(Px-y),
\]
expanding the squared Euclidean norm gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|x-y\|^2
&=\|x-Px\|^2
  +2(x-Px)^T(Px-y)
  +\|Px-y\|^2\\
&=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The second equality follows from the perpendicularity just proved.

The term \(\|x-Px\|^2\) does not depend on \(y\), and \(\|Px-y\|^2\) is nonnegative. Choosing \(y=Px\) makes the second term zero, so this choice attains the minimum. Any other minimizer would also have to satisfy
\[
\|Px-y\|^2=0,
\]
which implies \(y=Px\). The minimizer is therefore unique.

The permitted subspace may have dimension zero: when \(P=0\), we have \(S=\{0\}\), and the identity becomes
\[
\|x\|^2=\|x\|^2+0.
\]
When \(P\) is the identity matrix, \(S=\mathbb R^d\) and the residual \(x-Px\) is zero. The proof requires no inverse or rank assumption. Its conclusion concerns squared distance to the fixed subspace \(S\), rather than every possible layout constraint.

\]

\]

\[
\|x-y\|^2
=
\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2,
\]
where \(\|v\|^2=v^Tv\). The subspace \(S\) is allowed to have dimension zero.

**Proof.** Fix \(x\in\mathbb R^d\). The vector \(Px\) belongs to \(S\) by definition, so it is a permitted displacement. To compare it with any other \(y\in S\), write \(y=Pz\) for some \(z\in\mathbb R^d\). The hypothesis \(P^2=P\) gives
\[
Py=P(Pz)=P^2z=Pz=y.
\]
Thus applying \(P\) to a permitted displacement leaves it unchanged.

We split the difference \(x-y\) into two parts:
\[
x-y=(x-Px)+(Px-y).
\]
Write \(r=x-Px\) for the residual and \(u=Px-y\) for the difference between the two permitted displacements. Again using \(P^2=P\), together with \(Py=y\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
Pr&=Px-P^2x=Px-Px=0,\\
Pu&=P^2x-Py=Px-y=u.
\end{aligned}
\]
The symmetry hypothesis \(P^T=P\) now shows that these two parts are perpendicular:
\[
\begin{aligned}
r^Tu
&=r^T(Pu) &&\text{because }Pu=u\\
&=(P^Tr)^Tu &&\text{by the transpose rule}\\
&=(Pr)^Tu &&\text{because }P^T=P\\
&=0 &&\text{because }Pr=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Expanding the squared Euclidean norm therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|x-y\|^2
&=(r+u)^T(r+u)\\
&=r^Tr+r^Tu+u^Tr+u^Tu\\
&=\|r\|^2+\|u\|^2\\
&=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Both cross terms vanish because \(u^Tr=r^Tu=0\).

The first term is independent of \(y\), and the second is nonnegative. Taking \(y=Px\) makes the second term zero and attains the minimum. Any other minimizer must also satisfy
\[
\|Px-y\|^2=0,
\]
which implies \(y=Px\). This proves uniqueness.

When \(P=0\), we have \(S=\{0\}\), and the same proof and identity apply. When \(P\) is the identity matrix, \(Px=x\), so the residual is zero. The conclusion concerns squared distance to the fixed permitted subspace \(S\), not arbitrary layout constraints.

P(Px-y)
&=P^2x-Py\\
&=Px-y.
\end{aligned}
\]
The same hypothesis shows that \(P\) sends the residual \(x-Px\) to zero:
\[
P(x-Px)=Px-P^2x=0.
\]

We now use \(P^T=P\) to show that the residual is perpendicular to \(Px-y\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
(x-Px)^T(Px-y)
&=(x-Px)^TP(Px-y)\\
&=\bigl(P(x-Px)\bigr)^T(Px-y)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first equality uses \(P(Px-y)=Px-y\). For the second, symmetry gives
\[
(x-Px)^TP
=(x-Px)^TP^T
=\bigl(P(x-Px)\bigr)^T.
\]
The last equality uses \(P(x-Px)=0\).

Since
\[
x-y=(x-Px)+(Px-y),
\]
expanding the squared norm gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|x-y\|^2
&=\|x-Px\|^2
  +2(x-Px)^T(Px-y)
  +\|Px-y\|^2\\
&=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The cross term is zero by the calculation above.

The first term is independent of \(y\), and the second is nonnegative. Choosing \(y=Px\), which belongs to \(S\), makes the second term zero and therefore attains the minimum. Any other minimizer must also satisfy
\[
\|Px-y\|^2=0,
\]
which implies \(y=Px\). This proves uniqueness.

The argument includes the zero-dimensional case: if \(P=0\), then \(S=\{0\}\), and the identity becomes
\[
\|x-0\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|0\|^2.
\]
If \(P=I\), then \(S=\mathbb R^d\) and \(x-Px=0\). No inverse or rank assumption is needed. The conclusion concerns squared distance to the fixed subspace \(S\) defined above.

Claim. Let \(P\) be a real \(d\times d\) matrix, with \(d\geq 1\), such that \(P^2=P\) and \(P^T=P\). Let
\[
S=\{Pz:z\in\mathbb R^d\}
\]
be the set of permitted layout displacements. For every \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), the unique \(y\in S\) that minimizes \(\|x-y\|^2\) is \(Px\). In fact, for every \(y\in S\),
\[
\|x-y\|^2=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2,
\]
where \(\|v\|^2=v^Tv\).

Proof. The condition \(P^2=P\) implies \(P(Px)=Px\), so \(Px\in S\). Also, if \(y=Pz\in S\), then
\[
Py=P^2z=Pz=y.
\]
Thus \(P(Px-y)=Px-y\), while
\[
P(x-Px)=Px-P^2x=0.
\]
Using the symmetry condition \(P^T=P\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
(x-Px)^T(Px-y)
&=(x-Px)^TP(Px-y)\\
&=(P(x-Px))^T(Px-y)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first equality uses \(P(Px-y)=Px-y\); the second uses symmetry. Hence the two vectors \(x-Px\) and \(Px-y\) have zero inner product. Since \(x-y=(x-Px)+(Px-y)\), expanding the squared norm gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|x-y\|^2
&=\|(x-Px)+(Px-y)\|^2\\
&=\|x-Px\|^2+2(x-Px)^T(Px-y)+\|Px-y\|^2\\
&=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

The first term is independent of \(y\), and the second is nonnegative. It is zero when \(y=Px\), so \(Px\) minimizes the squared distance. If another \(y\in S\) attains the same minimum, then \(\|Px-y\|^2=0\), which implies \(y=Px\). This also covers the zero-dimensional permitted subspace: if \(P=0\), then \(S=\{0\}\), and the identity holds.

Focus lock keeps keyboard focus inside the current dialog until the dialog closes. It is useful when controls behind the dialog remain visible but should not receive keyboard input. Focus lock does not freeze the pointer, and it does not prevent the user from closing the dialog with the documented close command.

The implementation uses a sentinel at each end of the dialog's tab sequence. When focus reaches a sentinel, the handler moves it to the appropriate control at the opposite end. This is a focus-management mechanism, not a security boundary. Code running in the page can still move focus deliberately, so the application must handle those changes rather than assume the lock prevents them.

To test focus lock, open the dialog, traverse its controls in both directions, and close it while focus is on the last control. Focus should return to the control that opened the dialog. If that control has been removed, the application uses its documented fallback target. The fallback is part of the application's behavior and is not chosen by focus lock itself.

A separate hardware example describes a switch whose spring contacts latch when pressed. That use of latch refers to the physical mechanism. The example does not demonstrate the software feature and should not be used as a test of it.

Focus lock can help maintain a predictable keyboard sequence. It does not establish that labels, reading order, or announcements are correct; those require their own checks.

You will need the paper bridge, the tray, and the bag of counters from your group's box. Put the tray in the middle of the table and place the bridge across the tray. The bridge should rest on the two wooden blocks, not on the tray's rim. The tray is there to catch counters if they fall, so check that it sits under the middle of the bridge.

Before adding any counters, sketch the bridge from the side. Mark where the bridge touches the blocks. Then put one counter in the centre of the bridge and sketch the bridge again. Your second sketch should show the bridge, including any bend you can see, rather than just the new counter. If you cannot see a bend, say so beside the sketch.

Add counters one at a time, placing each on the same marked spot. After each addition, wait until the bridge stops moving before deciding whether to add another counter. The counters should stay in the tray if the bridge collapses. Do not rebuild the bridge during this first test, even if you have a promising idea about making it stronger.

When the test ends, count the counters that were on the bridge immediately before the bridge collapsed. If you stop because you have used all twelve counters and the bridge is still standing, record “held twelve; collapse not observed.” That is different from saying the bridge can hold exactly twelve.

Now discuss one change you would like to test next time. Keep your first sketches. These sketches record what this bridge did before the change, which will be useful when your next bridge behaves differently from the one you imagined.

The listening gallery offers two ways to hear the recorded accounts. You can use the fixed headphones beside each case, or borrow a receiver at the welcome desk to listen through the room’s induction loop. Receivers are free to borrow, and no booking is needed. We have six, so one may not be available immediately.

Every recording also has a printed transcript in the drawer beneath its case. The transcripts describe sounds that matter to the account, such as a bell or a pause interrupted by machinery, but not every background sound. Large-print copies are available at the welcome desk. You may take them into the gallery, but please return them before leaving.

At half past each hour, the room plays a three-minute sound sequence through its speakers. A light above the entrance comes on one minute before it begins. If you would rather avoid the sequence, you can leave through either doorway and return afterward. The recordings at the cases pause during the sequence, then resume from where they stopped.

On Wednesday mornings, from opening until noon, the speaker sequence is switched off. The case recordings and induction loop remain available. These mornings are quieter, but we cannot promise silence: people still talk, doors open, and school groups sometimes visit.

You are welcome to ask a gallery host for help with the equipment or for a seat. Hosts can explain the available options, though they cannot reserve a receiver or keep the room quiet for an individual visit. If you prefer to read before coming, you can request the same transcripts from the visitor team.
