In our survey of library use, 600 households were invited and 360 returned the initial questionnaire. Of these respondents, 252 reported using a library in the previous month, or 70 percent. The preliminary note described this as the percentage among initial respondents, but subsequent discussion sometimes treated it as the percentage among all 600 invited households. The initial responses alone did not establish that broader figure.

We then contacted initial nonrespondents by telephone. The budget covered 90 completed interviews, and interviewers stopped once they reached that number. These 90 households were not a simple random sample of the 240 initial nonrespondents: inclusion depended on whether interviewers could reach a household and whether it agreed to participate. Among the 90 interviewed households, 42 reported library use in the previous month, or approximately 46.7 percent.

Combining the two stages gives 294 reports of library use among 450 responding households, or approximately 65.3 percent. The follow-up therefore lowered the percentage observed among respondents from 70 to 65.3 percent by adding a group that reported less library use. This provides information about households absent from the initial results and shows that the two responding groups differed in their reports. Although both stages used the same question and reference month, households were not experimentally assigned to a survey mode. We therefore cannot tell how much of the difference reflects the people reached and how much reflects answering by telephone rather than by questionnaire.

The follow-up broadened the responding group, but 150 households still supplied no response. We do not know whether those households resemble either group that answered. Treating the combined percentage as an estimate for all 600 invitees would require assumptions about the remaining nonrespondents that were not evaluated here. No weights or imputed responses were used, so the follow-up should not be described as having statistically corrected the remaining nonresponse.

The report should present both stages and the combined figure, with each percentage clearly tied to the households who answered. The 65.3 percent figure describes a larger responding group and shows how the result changed with additional responses. It should accompany, rather than replace, the initial result, with the prevalence among all invited households still identified as unknown.

This preserves the concrete finding that reported library use was lower among the households reached in the follow-up, while making clear why the combined figure is not a final estimate for all invited households.

The drop from 70 to 65.3 percent reflects a change in the observed group: the initial respondents and the households reached for follow-up gave different reports. It does not establish the rate among all 600 invited households, because 150 did not respond. Nor can the difference show whether reports varied because of the people reached or the telephone mode.

The follow-up adds responses from households absent from the initial calculation, so it broadens the group described. But it does not establish that the remaining nonresponse has been corrected. No weights or imputed responses were used, and the study did not evaluate assumptions that would support such a correction.

The report should present both stages and the combined percentage as a description of the 450 responding households, not as a final estimate for all invited households. The follow-up shows how the reported percentage changed when another group answered. We do not know whether the 150 households still missing would report library use at a rate closer to either responding group.

We started by counting how often the date field was filled. But a year in the field was not necessarily supported by the card, and an empty field could mean that the date was absent, unreadable, or overlooked. Before using field completion to judge the transcription, we needed to distinguish these cases.

We selected eighty catalogue cards from a single drawer that had not yet been entered into the digital index. Two staff members transcribed each card independently. They could enter a year, mark the date as absent, or mark it as unreadable. The instructions did not allow them to infer a year. We later inspected the cards together and recorded a reference decision for each one. This gave us an internally reconciled record for the trial, rather than an independent external check of the dates.

In that record, fifty cards had a readable year, eighteen had no date, and twelve had an unreadable date. The first transcriber entered the reference year on forty-seven of the fifty readable cards and marked three as unreadable. The second entered the reference year on forty-nine and marked one as unreadable. Neither entered a year on any of the thirty cards whose dates were absent or unreadable in the reconciled record. On those thirty cards, the transcribers agreed with each other about whether the date was absent or unreadable on twenty-six. We have not tabulated how often each transcriber's decisions on that distinction agreed with the reconciled record.

Judging the work only by the proportion of cards containing a year would make both transcribers' records look substantially incomplete. Yet on thirty cards, the procedure required an entry other than a year. Counting years alone would also hide the four disagreements about why no year was entered. Those disagreements could matter when someone returned to the cards. A reader trying to find a document's date needs different information from a conservator deciding whether another imaging method might make a date readable.

We chose the drawer for convenience, so these counts describe this trial and do not estimate error across the collection. They suggest that we should report readable-year transcription separately from decisions about whether dates are missing or unreadable. That would make clearer what we counted. We have not tested whether it would improve later retrieval.

We should repeat the pond survey this season before describing the lower count as a population decline. Requesting another survey does not mean postponing action. It is a step we can take now to improve the information available for the advisory meeting next month.

Last year’s team visited each of eight ponds twice at dusk. This year’s team visited the same ponds once at midday and recorded fewer animals in total. No adjustment has been made for visit frequency or time of day, and the records do not contain enough information to reconstruct the missed dusk visits. We therefore know that the recorded total was lower, but we cannot read the size of a population change directly from the difference between the totals.

A drainage proposal affecting three of the surveyed ponds makes better information about their condition relevant to an upcoming decision. The proposal does not explain the lower count, especially since drainage has not begun. Nor does the approaching meeting make the two surveys more comparable. It gives us a reason to address the uncertainty promptly.

We recommend two dusk visits to each pond, using the earlier recording sheet. Matching the previous survey’s visit frequency, time of day, and recording sheet would make the new observations more comparable with last year’s, although weather and detectability would still vary. The repeat survey would not isolate the effect of drainage or provide a population census. Its immediate purpose is to reduce an avoidable ambiguity in the evidence available to the meeting: whether the difference in totals reflects, at least in part, the different survey methods.

If the repeat survey cannot be completed before the meeting, the advisory note should report the lower observed total together with the differences in survey effort and timing, and describe the planned work as pending. The current record supports neither a confident estimate of population decline nor a confident assurance of stability. We should judge the monitoring request by whether it would improve the information available for the pending decision, without requiring it to support either conclusion in advance.

We recommend keeping completed interviews in the weekly dashboard while ending the practice of ranking interviewers by that number alone. The count tells us whether fieldwork is moving, but it does not tell us enough to compare people whose assigned routes differ.

Some routes contain apartment buildings with a staffed entrance. Others contain scattered homes that require long walks between attempts. Assignments rotate each month, but the dashboard ranks interviewers each week. Rotation may spread difficult routes over a longer period without making any particular week's assignments comparable. We have not estimated how large that difference is.

The ranking also leaves out work that does not produce a completed interview. A careful refusal record or a return visit at the requested time may be necessary fieldwork even when no questionnaire is completed. Including those activities in the discussion would not mean treating every attempt as equally useful. Supervisors would still need to look at what happened and whether the agreed contact procedure was followed.

We do not propose replacing the ranking with a single weighted score. We have no tested weights, and a score could conceal the same judgment inside a formula. For the next four weeks, the dashboard should show completed interviews, attempts, and route assignments together. Supervisors should add a brief explanation when discussing unusual totals.

This arrangement will take more attention than reading a league table, and that cost is part of the recommendation. It may also reveal problems that the old ranking missed, but we cannot claim that it will improve response rates before trying it. At the end of four weeks, the steering group should ask whether the added context led to useful changes in supervisory decisions and whether the burden was manageable. The aim is to make the weekly discussion more informative while preserving a clear view of fieldwork progress.

Let \(N\geq 2\), and let \(y_1,\ldots,y_N\) be fixed real responses. Write
\[
\mu=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i,
\qquad
\sigma^2=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mu)^2.
\]
Choose an unordered pair \(P\) uniformly from the \(\binom{N}{2}\) pairs, then choose \(J\) uniformly from the two indices in \(P\). Set
\[
Y=y_J,
\qquad
Z=\frac12\sum_{i\in P}y_i.
\]
We will show that
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]
All expectations and variances refer to repeated sampling from this fixed population.

Each index belongs to \(N-1\) pairs. Thus, for every \(i\),
\[
\mathbb P(J=i)
=\sum_{j\ne i}\mathbb P(P=\{i,j\})
  \mathbb P(J=i\mid P=\{i,j\})
=\frac{N-1}{2\binom{N}{2}}
=\frac1N.
\]
It follows that
\[
\mathbb E[Y]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2.
\]

Conditional on \(P=\{i,j\}\), the variable \(Y\) takes the values \(y_i\) and \(y_j\) with equal probabilities, so
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{y_i+y_j}{2}.
\]
The right-hand side is the value of \(Z\) for this pair. Hence
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z,
\qquad
\mathbb E[Z]
=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[Y\mid P]\right]
=\mathbb E[Y]
=\mu.
\]

To compute the variance, write
\[
Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu).
\]
Because \(Z\) is determined by \(P\),
\[
\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]
=\mathbb E[Y\mid P]-Z
=0.
\]
Conditioning on \(P\) therefore makes the mixed term vanish:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)\mid P]\right]\\
&=\mathbb E\!\left[(Z-\mu)\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]\right]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Expanding the square and using \(\mathbb E[Z]=\mu\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2
&=\mathbb E[(Y-\mu)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
  +2\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
  +\mathbb E[(Z-\mu)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z).
\end{aligned}
\]
The mixed term is zero because the conditional mean of \(Y-Z\) is zero. This does not require \(Y\) and \(Z\) to be independent.

For a given pair \(P=\{i,j\}\), the two possible values of \(Y-Z\) are \((y_i-y_j)/2\) and its negative. Thus
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4},
\]
and averaging over the uniformly chosen pairs yields
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
=\frac{1}{4\binom{N}{2}}
  \sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2.
\]
To evaluate the sum, expand each square:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
&=(N-1)\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2-2\sum_{i<j}y_i y_j\\
&=N\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2-\left(\sum_{i=1}^N y_i\right)^2\\
&=N\left(\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2-N\mu^2\right)\\
&=N\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mu)^2\\
&=N^2\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first equality uses the fact that each \(y_i^2\) appears in \(N-1\) pairs. Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
=\frac{N^2\sigma^2}{4\binom{N}{2}}
=\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)}.
\]
Substituting into the variance decomposition gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Z)
=\sigma^2-\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)}
=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]

When \(N=2\), the pair is the full population and \(Z=\mu\) is constant. If all responses coincide, both variances vanish for every \(N\). The argument covers both cases without dividing by \(\sigma^2\).

Let \(N\geq 2\), and let \(y_1,\ldots,y_N\) be fixed real responses. Write
\[
\mu=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i,
\qquad

\]
We will show that
\[

\qquad

\]
All expectations and variances refer to repeated sampling from this fixed population.

Conditional on \(P=\{i,j\}\), the random variable \(Y\) takes the values \(y_i\) and \(y_j\) with equal probabilities, while \(Z=(y_i+y_j)/2\). Thus
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z,
\qquad

\]
The two possible values of \(Y-Z\) are \((y_i-y_j)/2\) and its negative, so
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
\]

To find the marginal distribution of \(J\), note that each index \(i\) belongs to \(N-1\) pairs. Hence
\[
\Pr(J=i)
=\sum_{j\ne i}\Pr(P=\{i,j\})\Pr(J=i\mid P=\{i,j\})
=\frac{N-1}{2\binom{N}{2}}
=\frac1N.
\]
It follows that
\[
\mathbb E[Y]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2.
\]
Taking expectations in \(\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z\) now gives
\[
\mathbb E[Z]
=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[Y\mid P]\right]
=\mathbb E[Y]
=\mu.
\]

We next decompose the variance of \(Y\). Since \(Z-\mu\) is determined by \(P\), it can be taken outside the conditional expectation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)\mid P]\right]\\
&=\mathbb E\!\left[(Z-\mu)\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]\right]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The mixed term vanishes because \(Y-Z\) has conditional mean zero given \(P\). This is an orthogonality relation and does not require independence of \(Y\) and \(Z\).

Using \(Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu)\), we therefore obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2
&=\mathbb E[(Y-\mu)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
  +2\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
  +\mathbb E[(Z-\mu)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z).
\end{aligned}
\]

To evaluate the remaining expectation, first observe that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
&=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N(y_i-y_j)^2\\
&=N\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2-\left(\sum_{i=1}^N y_i\right)^2\\
&=N\left(\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2-N\mu^2\right)\\
&=N\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mu)^2\\
&=N^2\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Averaging the conditional second moment over the uniformly chosen pairs gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2\mid P]\right]\\
&=\frac{1}{4\binom{N}{2}}\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2\\
&=\frac{N^2\sigma^2}{4\binom{N}{2}}\\
&=\frac{N}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Z)
=\sigma^2-\frac{N}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2
=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]

When \(N=2\), the pair is the full population and \(Z=\mu\) is constant. If all responses coincide, both \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\) vanish for every \(N\). The argument covers these cases without dividing by \(\sigma^2\).

\]
All expectations and variances refer to repeated sampling from this fixed population.

Each index \(i\) belongs to \(N-1\) pairs. Therefore
\[
\Pr(J=i)
=\sum_{j\ne i}\Pr(P=\{i,j\})\Pr(J=i\mid P=\{i,j\})
=\frac{N-1}{2\binom N2}
=\frac1N.
\]
Thus
\[
\mathbb E[Y]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2.
\]

Conditional on \(P=\{i,j\}\), the variable \(Y\) takes \(y_i\) and \(y_j\) with equal probabilities, so
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{y_i+y_j}{2}
=Z.
\]
Taking expectations gives
\[
\mathbb E[Z]
=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[Y\mid P]\right]
=\mathbb E[Y]
=\mu.
\]

To relate the variances, write
\[
Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu).
\]
The mixed term has expectation zero. Indeed, \(Z-\mu\) is determined by \(P\), and
\[
\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]
=\mathbb E[Y\mid P]-Z
=0.
\]
Hence, by conditioning on \(P\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)\mid P]\right]\\
&=\mathbb E\!\left[(Z-\mu)\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]\right]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Expanding the square and using \(\mathbb E[Z]=\mu\) now gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2
&=\mathbb E[(Y-\mu)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
  +2\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
  +\mathbb E[(Z-\mu)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z).
\end{aligned}
\]
This calculation uses conditional expectations and does not require \(Y\) and \(Z\) to be independent.

It remains to compute \(\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]\). Given \(P=\{i,j\}\), the two possible values of \(Y-Z\) are \((y_i-y_j)/2\) and its negative. Thus
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
\]
The required sum satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
&=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N(y_i-y_j)^2\\
&=N\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2-\left(\sum_{i=1}^N y_i\right)^2\\
&=N\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mu)^2\\
&=N^2\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Averaging over the uniformly chosen pair therefore yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
&=\frac{1}{4\binom N2}\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2\\
&=\frac{N^2\sigma^2}{4\binom N2}\\
&=\frac{N}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting into the variance decomposition gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Z)
=\sigma^2-\frac{N}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2
=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]

When \(N=2\), the pair is the full population and \(Z=\mu\) is constant. If all responses coincide, both variances vanish for every \(N\). The derivation includes these cases because it never divides by \(\sigma^2\).

Let \(N\ge 2\), and let \(y_1,\ldots,y_N\) be fixed real responses. Define
\[
\mu=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i,
\qquad
\sigma^2=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i-\mu)^2.
\]
Choose an unordered pair \(P\) uniformly from the \(\binom{N}{2}\) pairs, then choose \(J\) uniformly from the two indices in \(P\). Set
\[
Y=y_J,
\qquad
Z=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\in P} y_i.
\]
Then
\[
\mathbb{E}[Z]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]
These variances describe repeated sampling from the fixed population; the responses themselves are not random.

For \(P=\{i,j\}\), the conditional distribution of \(Y\) assigns probability \(1/2\) to each of \(y_i\) and \(y_j\). Hence
\[
\mathbb{E}[Y\mid P]=\frac{y_i+y_j}{2}=Z,
\]
and
\[
\mathbb{E}[(Y-Z)^2\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
\]
Each index belongs to \(N-1\) of the \(\binom{N}{2}\) pairs. Since \(J\) is chosen uniformly within its pair, each index has probability
\[
\frac{N-1}{\binom{N}{2}}\cdot\frac12=\frac1N
\]
of being selected. Thus \(Y\) is uniform over the population, so \(\mathbb{E}[Y]=\mu\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2\). Taking expectations in \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid P]=Z\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[Z]=\mu\).

Because \(Z\) is determined by \(P\), the conditional expectation identity also gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
&=\mathbb{E}\!\left[(Z-\mu)\mathbb{E}[Y-Z\mid P]\right]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Now write \(Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu)\) and expand the square. The mixed term has expectation zero, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2
=\operatorname{Var}(Y)
&=\mathbb{E}[(Y-\mu)^2]\\
&=\mathbb{E}[(Y-Z)^2]+\mathbb{E}[(Z-\mu)^2]\\
&=\mathbb{E}[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z).
\end{aligned}
\]
This orthogonality follows from conditioning on \(P\); it does not require \(Y\) and \(Z\) to be independent.

To compute the first term, use the finite identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
&=N\sum_i y_i^2-\left(\sum_i y_i\right)^2\\
&=N\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2\\
&=N^2\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Averaging the conditional squared deviations over the uniformly selected pair gives
\[
\mathbb{E}[(Y-Z)^2]
=\frac{1}{4\binom{N}{2}}\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
=\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Z)
=\sigma^2-\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)}
=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]
When \(N=2\), \(P\) is the full population and \(Z\) is constant, as the formula gives. If all responses coincide, both variances are zero for every \(N\); the derivation does not divide by \(\sigma^2\).

Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{r\times d}\), and suppose
\[
y=Ax+e,\qquad \|e\|_2\leq\varepsilon,\qquad \varepsilon\geq0.
\]
Define \(K=\ker A\), and let \(P\) be the orthogonal projection onto \(K^\perp\). Assume that \(\gamma>0\) and
\[
\|Av\|_2\geq\gamma\|v\|_2
\qquad\text{for every }v\in K^\perp.
\]
For any least-squares minimizer \(\hat x\) of \(\|Az-y\|_2\), which exists in finite dimensions, we claim that
\[
\|P(\hat x-x)\|_2\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma}.
\]

To prove this, put \(h=\hat x-x\). The normal equations and the identity \(y=Ax+e\) give
\[
A^\top(A\hat x-y)=A^\top(Ah-e)=0.
\]
Multiplying on the left by \(h^\top\) and applying Cauchy–Schwarz yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|Ah\|_2^2
&=\langle Ah,e\rangle\\
&\leq\|Ah\|_2\|e\|_2\\
&\leq\varepsilon\|Ah\|_2.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(Ah\neq0\), division by \(\|Ah\|_2\) gives \(\|Ah\|_2\leq\varepsilon\). This bound also holds when \(Ah=0\).

We cannot apply the assumed lower bound directly to \(h\), but we can apply it to \(Ph\in K^\perp\). Indeed, the orthogonal decomposition
\[
h=Ph+(I-P)h
\]
has \((I-P)h\in K\), so
\[
Ah=APh+A(I-P)h=APh.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\gamma\|Ph\|_2
\leq\|APh\|_2
=\|Ah\|_2
\leq\varepsilon.
\]
Dividing by \(\gamma>0\) proves the claimed bound.

When \(\varepsilon=0\), the bound gives \(P\hat x=Px\), so the observable component is recovered exactly. This does not imply uniqueness of \(\hat x\): adding any vector in \(K\) leaves its least-squares objective unchanged. If \(K^\perp=\{0\}\), then \(P=0\), and the bound holds trivially. No bound on the error component in \(K\) follows from these assumptions.

\[

\]

\[

\]

\[

=\langle Ah,e\rangle
\le \|Ah\|_2\|e\|_2

\[
h=Ph+(I-P)h,
\qquad Ph\in K^\perp,\qquad (I-P)h\in K.
\]
Since \(A(I-P)h=0\), we have \(Ah=APh\). Thus
\[

\le \|APh\|_2
=\|Ah\|_2
\le \varepsilon,
\]
which proves the claim.

When \(\varepsilon=0\), this gives \(P\widehat x=Px\), so the observable component is recovered exactly. It does not imply uniqueness of \(\widehat x\), since adding any vector in \(K\) leaves the fitted observation unchanged. If \(K^\perp=\{0\}\), then \(P=0\) and the claimed bound holds trivially. Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{r\times d}\), let \(y=Ax+e\), and suppose \(\|e\|_2\le\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon\ge0\). Set \(K=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:Av=0\}\), and let \(P\) be the orthogonal projection onto \(K^\perp\). Assume \(\gamma>0\) and
\[
\|Av\|_2\ge\gamma\|v\|_2
\qquad\text{for every }v\in K^\perp.
\]
For any least-squares minimizer \(\hat x\) of \(\|Az-y\|_2\), we claim
\[
\|P(\hat x-x)\|_2\le\frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma}.
\]
This bounds only the observable component of the estimation error.

A least-squares minimizer exists in finite dimensions and satisfies the normal equations
\[
A^\top(A\hat x-y)=0.
\]
Writing \(h=\hat x-x\) and using \(y=Ax+e\), we get
\[
A^\top(Ah-e)=0.
\]
Multiplying by \(h^\top\) gives
\[
\|Ah\|_2^2=\langle Ah,e\rangle\le \|Ah\|_2\,\varepsilon.
\]
If \(Ah\ne0\), division by \(\|Ah\|_2\) yields \(\|Ah\|_2\le\varepsilon\); if \(Ah=0\), the same bound holds directly.

Decompose \(h=Ph+(I-P)h\). Since \((I-P)h\in K\), we have \(A(I-P)h=0\), and hence \(Ah=A(Ph)\). Also \(Ph\in K^\perp\), so the assumed lower bound applies to \(Ph\):
\[
\gamma\|Ph\|_2\le\|A(Ph)\|_2=\|Ah\|_2\le\varepsilon.
\]
Thus \(\|P(\hat x-x)\|_2\le\varepsilon/\gamma\).

When \(\varepsilon=0\), this proves \(P(\hat x-x)=0\), so the observable component is recovered exactly; it does not imply that \(\hat x\) is unique. If \(K^\perp=\{0\}\), then \(P=0\), and the claimed bound holds trivially.

The case contains a facsimile of the workshop ledger. The original is kept in controlled storage because repeated exposure to light would make its faded entries harder to read. A facsimile reproduces a particular object; a reconstruction attempts to supply something missing. This display uses the first approach. Gaps in the original remain gaps in the copy.

The pages are reproduced at their original size. The paper is modern and has not been artificially aged. We chose it for contrast and durability, not to make a visitor believe it had survived a century in the workshop. A small label on every opening identifies the copy, so visitors who enter halfway along the case receive the same information as those who start at the beginning.

The transcription beside the facsimile expands common abbreviations in square brackets. An uncertain reading is followed by a question mark. These conventions separate a proposed reading from a clear one, but they cannot convey every hesitation made during transcription. Readers who want to compare the handwriting can use the facing image.

A two-week trial of the display has ended. During the trial, hosts recorded which labels visitors asked about and whether visitors noticed that the ledger was a copy. The observations will be discussed now that the trial has ended. They will inform a later decision about the labels; the trial itself does not commit the museum to changing them.

At the start of each shift, place the probe in the reference fixture and record its reading. The acceptance band is 48 to 52 units, including both endpoints. This check compares the probe with a stable reference block. It does not measure the temperature of material currently on the line, and a reading inside the band does not by itself authorize a production restart.

During the six-week trial, if the first reference-block reading is outside the acceptance band, let the probe rest in the fixture for ten minutes, then repeat the reading once. This rest period applies only before the repeat reading. Record both readings in the shift log before making any call required by this rule. If the repeat is also outside the band, call the shift lead. If the repeat is within the band, no call is required by this rule. The lead will decide whether a further check is needed. Do not change the probe's offset in response to this check. The trial concerns the escalation process, not permission for operators to recalibrate the instrument.

For the weekly trend chart, use the first reading from each shift, including first readings outside the acceptance band. Keep any repeat readings in the log, but do not substitute them into the chart. This keeps the plotted sequence tied to the same point in the checking process, even when the escalation procedure calls for more than one observation.

The maintenance team will review the log and the chart at the end of the trial. A charted outlier is a reason to examine the record, not a diagnosis of a failed probe. Please include notes about a loose fixture or an interrupted check where relevant. Those notes help explain what happened, but they do not replace the numerical readings.
